q: Gregor Mendel carried out his famous breeding experiments on which plant?
x: Mendel worked with the garden pea, Pisum sativum. It has clear contrasting traits, is easy to grow and normally self-pollinates, so pure lines are easy to keep.

q: How many pairs of contrasting characters of the pea plant did Mendel study?
x: Mendel studied seven characters, such as stem height, seed shape, seed colour, pod shape, pod colour, flower colour and flower position, each with two clear contrasting forms.

q: Which feature of the pea plant made it especially suitable for Mendel's experiments?
o: It has a very long life cycle, giving time to observe each plant
Its traits show continuous variation that can be measured
Its flowers normally self-pollinate, so pure-breeding lines are easy to maintain
It produces only a few seeds in each generation
x: Pea flowers normally self-pollinate, so true-breeding lines are kept easily, yet they can be cross-pollinated by hand. Peas also have a short life cycle, many seeds and sharply contrasting (not continuous) traits.

q: Alternative forms of a gene that occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes are called:
x: Alleles are different forms of the same gene, such as T (tall) and t (dwarf), found at the same locus on a pair of homologous chromosomes.

q: Which statement correctly expresses Mendel's law of segregation?
o: The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one
Alleles of different genes are distributed to gametes independently of one another
In a heterozygote, only the dominant allele is passed on to the gametes
The two alleles of a gene blend in the hybrid and cannot be separated again
x: The law of segregation says the paired alleles separate at gamete formation, so each gamete is pure for one allele. Independent assortment of different genes is Mendel's second law, not the first.

q: The law of segregation is explained by which event of meiosis?
o: Separation of sister chromatids in mitotic anaphase
Replication of DNA in the S phase
Pairing of non-homologous chromosomes in prophase II
Separation of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I
x: The two alleles of a gene lie on a pair of homologous chromosomes. When the homologues separate in anaphase I of meiosis, the alleles go to different gametes.

q: Mendel crossed a pure tall pea plant (TT) with a pure dwarf plant (tt). The F1 plants were:
x: Every F1 plant receives T from one parent and t from the other, so all are Tt. Tall is dominant, so all F1 plants are tall.

q: In the F2 of a monohybrid cross between pure tall (TT) and pure dwarf (tt) pea plants, the genotypic ratio is:
x: Selfing Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. The phenotypic ratio is 3 tall : 1 dwarf because TT and Tt both look tall.

q: In the F2 of a cross between pure tall (TT) and pure dwarf (tt) pea plants, what fraction of the tall plants are heterozygous?
x: The F2 is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Of the three tall parts, two are Tt, so 2/3 of tall plants are heterozygous. The value 1/2 is the fraction of all F2 plants that are heterozygous.

q: A test cross is a cross between an individual of dominant phenotype and:
o: One of its own F2 offspring chosen at random
x: In a test cross the unknown dominant-looking individual is crossed with a homozygous recessive. The recessive parent gives only recessive alleles, so the offspring reveal the unknown genotype.

q: A heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) is test crossed. The expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring is:
x: Tt × tt gives half Tt (tall) and half tt (dwarf), a 1 : 1 ratio. A 3 : 1 ratio comes from selfing Tt, not from a test cross.

q: A tall pea plant is test crossed and all 120 offspring are tall. The genotype of the tall parent is:
o: Either TT or Tt, with equal chance
x: If the parent were Tt, about half the offspring of the test cross would be dwarf. All tall offspring show the parent gave only T gametes, so it is homozygous TT.

q: The term 'phenotype' refers to:
o: The genetic constitution of an organism
The observable characteristics of an organism
The set of alleles carried in one gamete
The position of a gene on a chromosome
x: Phenotype is what can be seen or measured, such as tall or dwarf. Genotype is the genetic make-up (TT, Tt, tt), and the position of a gene is its locus.

q: Which statement about a homozygous recessive pea plant (tt) is correct?
o: It produces T and t gametes in equal numbers
It produces only one type of gamete, all carrying t
It gives a 3 : 1 ratio when self-pollinated
x: A tt plant has two identical alleles, so all its gametes carry t, and it breeds true for dwarfness. Only a heterozygote (Tt) makes two kinds of gametes and gives 3 : 1 on selfing.

q: Crossing an F1 hybrid with either of its parents (dominant or recessive) is called a:
x: A back cross is a cross of the F1 with one of its parents. When that parent is the homozygous recessive one, the back cross also serves as a test cross.

q: An F1 tall plant (Tt) is back crossed with its homozygous tall parent (TT). The offspring will be:
o: All tall; half TT and half Tt
x: TT gives only T gametes and Tt gives T and t equally, so offspring are 1 TT : 1 Tt. Both genotypes are tall, so no dwarf plants appear.

q: In complete dominance, the heterozygote (Tt) shows:
o: A phenotype intermediate between the two parents
The phenotypes of both alleles side by side
The same phenotype as the homozygous recessive
The same phenotype as the homozygous dominant
x: With complete dominance the dominant allele fully masks the recessive one, so Tt looks just like TT. An intermediate heterozygote is incomplete dominance; both alleles shown together is codominance.

q: In the four o'clock plant, red flower × white flower gives pink F1. If the F1 plants are crossed among themselves, the F2 phenotypic ratio is:
x: This is incomplete dominance. Selfing the pink heterozygote gives 1 homozygous red : 2 pink : 1 homozygous white, so the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio, 1 : 2 : 1.

q: A person with the genotype IᴬIᴮ has both A and B antigens on the red blood cells. This is an example of:
x: In codominance both alleles of the heterozygote are fully expressed, so IᴬIᴮ gives blood group AB. In incomplete dominance the heterozygote would be intermediate instead.

q: Two parents are both heterozygous (Aa) for a gene. What is the probability that a child will be homozygous recessive (aa)?
x: Each parent passes a with probability 1/2, so aa has probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. This is the recessive quarter of the 3 : 1 ratio.

q: Albinism is an autosomal recessive trait. Two normally pigmented parents are both carriers (Aa). What is the probability that both of their first two children will be albino?
x: Each child independently has a 1/4 chance of being aa. For both children, multiply: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

q: From the cross Aa × Aa, what proportion of the offspring is expected to be heterozygous?
x: The offspring are 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so 2/4 = 1/2 are heterozygous. The value 2/3 applies only to the dominant-looking offspring, not to all offspring.

q: Which of the following pea traits studied by Mendel is recessive?
x: Round seed is dominant over wrinkled, so wrinkled is recessive. Yellow seed, tall stem and inflated pod were all dominant in Mendel's crosses.

q: Which of the following pea traits studied by Mendel is dominant?
x: In pea, green pod is dominant over yellow pod. Note the difference with seeds: yellow seed is dominant over green seed. Terminal flowers and constricted pods are recessive.

q: A 'pure-breeding' (true-breeding) plant is one that:
o: Is homozygous and gives offspring like itself when self-pollinated
Is heterozygous and shows the dominant trait
Always produces two types of gametes
Gives a 3 : 1 ratio in the next generation
x: A true-breeding plant is homozygous (TT or tt), so on selfing all its offspring show the same trait. Mendel started each experiment with such pure lines.

q: How many different types of gametes can a pea plant of genotype TT produce?
x: A homozygote has two identical alleles, so every gamete carries T: only one type. A heterozygote (Tt) would produce two types.

q: Mendel crossed tall females with dwarf males and also dwarf females with tall males. In both crosses the F1 plants were:
x: These are reciprocal crosses. Both gave all-tall F1, showing that the result did not depend on which parent was male or female; only dominance decided the F1 phenotype.

q: To obtain the F2 generation in his monohybrid experiments, Mendel:
o: Crossed the F1 plants with the recessive parent
Crossed the F1 plants with the dominant parent
Crossed the two original parents again
Allowed the F1 plants to self-pollinate
x: Mendel let the F1 hybrids self-pollinate to get the F2, where the recessive trait reappeared in about one quarter of the plants. Crossing F1 with a parent is a back cross.

q: In a monohybrid cross, the F2 contains 800 plants. About how many are expected to be dwarf (tt)?
x: The F2 phenotypic ratio is 3 tall : 1 dwarf, so 1/4 are dwarf: 800 ÷ 4 = 200. The 600 would be the tall plants.

q: A tall pea plant is self-pollinated and gives 75 tall and 25 dwarf offspring. The genotype of the parent plant is:
o: It cannot be decided from this result
x: A 3 : 1 ratio on selfing appears only when the parent is heterozygous, Tt. A TT plant would give only tall offspring, and a tt plant only dwarf offspring.

q: In guinea pigs, black coat (B) is dominant over white (b). Two black guinea pigs produce a white offspring. The genotypes of the parents must be:
o: Either BB × Bb or Bb × Bb
x: A white offspring is bb, so it got b from each parent. Both black parents therefore carry b and must be Bb. A cross involving BB could never give a bb offspring.

q: Mendel called the trait that disappeared in the F1 but reappeared in the F2:
x: A recessive trait is masked in the heterozygous F1 and shows again in the F2 in about one quarter of the plants. The trait seen in the F1 is the dominant one.

q: Mendel formulated the law of independent assortment from the results of:
x: Independent assortment concerns two or more genes at once, so it came from dihybrid crosses, such as seed shape with seed colour. Monohybrid crosses gave the law of segregation.

q: Which statement correctly expresses the law of independent assortment?
o: The two alleles of one gene separate into different gametes
Genes on the same chromosome are always inherited together
Alleles of different genes are sorted into gametes independently of one another
In a heterozygote, one allele masks the effect of the other
x: The law says the separation of one pair of alleles does not affect the separation of another pair. The separation of the two alleles of one gene is the law of segregation.

q: In Mendel's dihybrid cross (round yellow × wrinkled green), the F2 phenotypic ratio was:
x: Selfing the RrYy F1 gives 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. A 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio comes from a dihybrid test cross.

q: A pea plant of genotype RrYy forms gametes. What is the probability that a gamete carries both r and y?
x: With independent assortment, each gamete gets r with probability 1/2 and y with probability 1/2, so ry = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The four gamete types RY, Ry, rY and ry are equally likely.

q: How many different types of gametes are produced by a pea plant of genotype RrYy?
x: RrYy forms RY, Ry, rY and ry, four types in equal numbers. The 16 is the number of boxes in the Punnett square when two such plants are crossed.

q: What types of gametes does a plant of genotype RRYy produce?
x: The R gene is homozygous, so every gamete has R; the Y gene is heterozygous, giving Y or y. So the gametes are RY and Ry. A gamete carries one allele of each gene, never two of the same gene.

q: How many different types of gametes are formed by an individual of genotype AaBbCc, if all three genes assort independently?
x: The number of gamete types is 2ⁿ, where n is the number of heterozygous gene pairs. With three heterozygous pairs, 2³ = 8.

q: How many different types of gametes can an individual of genotype AaBBCcDd produce, if all four genes assort independently?
x: Only the heterozygous pairs add variety. Aa, Cc and Dd are heterozygous and BB is not, so there are 2³ = 8 gamete types, not 2⁴ = 16.

q: In the F2 of a cross between pure round yellow (RRYY) and wrinkled green (rryy) peas, what fraction shows round yellow seeds?
x: Round yellow plants have at least one R and one Y: 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16. This is the '9' of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

q: In the F2 of a dihybrid cross between RRYY and rryy pea plants, what fraction of the plants is wrinkled green?
x: Wrinkled green plants must be rryy: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. They are the single double-recessive class of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

q: Pure round yellow (RRYY) peas are crossed with wrinkled green (rryy). In the F2, what fraction shows a combination of traits not found in either parent?
x: The new combinations are round green (3/16) and wrinkled yellow (3/16), together 6/16 = 3/8. Round yellow and wrinkled green are the parental combinations.

q: How many different genotypes appear in the F2 of a dihybrid cross (RrYy × RrYy)?
x: Each gene gives three genotypes (RR, Rr, rr and YY, Yy, yy), so there are 3 × 3 = 9 genotypes. There are only 4 phenotypes, and 16 is the number of gamete combinations.

q: How many different phenotypes appear in the F2 of a dihybrid cross showing complete dominance for both genes?
x: With complete dominance each gene gives two phenotypes, so 2 × 2 = 4 phenotypes (round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow, wrinkled green). The 9 is the number of genotypes.

q: A round yellow pea plant (RrYy) is crossed with a wrinkled green plant (rryy). The expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring is:
x: This dihybrid test cross gives RrYy, Rryy, rrYy and rryy equally, because RrYy forms four equal gamete types and rryy forms only ry. Hence 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.

q: A round yellow pea plant is crossed with a wrinkled green (rryy) plant. The offspring are round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green in equal numbers. The round yellow parent was:
x: Equal numbers of four classes show that the round yellow parent formed four kinds of gametes, so it was heterozygous for both genes. RRYY would give only round yellow offspring.

q: In the F2 of a dihybrid cross (RrYy × RrYy), what fraction of the plants is homozygous for both genes?
x: The genotypes homozygous at both loci are RRYY, RRyy, rrYY and rryy, each 1/16, giving 4/16 = 1/4. Equivalently, 1/2 homozygous for R × 1/2 homozygous for Y = 1/4.

q: In the F2 of a dihybrid cross (RrYy × RrYy), what proportion of the offspring has the genotype RrYy?
x: The chance of Rr is 1/2 and of Yy is 1/2, so RrYy = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 (4 of the 16 boxes). The 9/16 is the round yellow phenotype, which includes several genotypes.

q: In the F2 of a dihybrid cross (RrYy × RrYy), what proportion of the plants is RRYY?
x: RR has probability 1/4 and YY has probability 1/4, so RRYY = 1/16. It is only one of the four genotypes inside the round yellow class.

q: The cytological basis of independent assortment is:
o: The separation of sister chromatids at anaphase II
The random orientation of different homologous pairs at metaphase I
The replication of DNA before meiosis
x: Each bivalent lines up at metaphase I independently of the others, so which maternal or paternal chromosome goes to a pole is random for each pair. Genes on different pairs therefore assort independently.

q: The law of independent assortment holds for genes that are:
o: Located close together on the same chromosome
Always found on the X chromosome
x: Independent assortment depends on genes lying on different chromosome pairs, which orient independently in meiosis. Genes close together on one chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together.

q: In peas, a plant RrYy is crossed with a plant rrYy. What fraction of the offspring is expected to be wrinkled yellow?
x: Rr × rr gives rr (wrinkled) with probability 1/2; Yy × Yy gives yellow (Y_) with probability 3/4. Wrinkled yellow = 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8.

q: Genes A/a and B/b assort independently with complete dominance. The cross AaBb × Aabb gives which phenotypic ratio (A_B_ : A_bb : aaB_ : aabb)?
x: Aa × Aa gives 3/4 A_ and 1/4 aa; Bb × bb gives 1/2 B_ and 1/2 bb. Multiplying: A_B_ 3/8, A_bb 3/8, aaB_ 1/8, aabb 1/8, which is 3 : 3 : 1 : 1.

q: A dihybrid cross (RrYy × RrYy) produces 160 plants. About how many are expected to be round green?
x: Round green is 3/16 of the F2: 3/16 × 160 = 30. The 90 would be round yellow (9/16) and 10 would be wrinkled green (1/16).

q: Among the round yellow plants in the F2 of a dihybrid cross (RrYy × RrYy), what fraction is true-breeding for both traits (RRYY)?
x: Round yellow plants make up 9 of the 16 boxes, and only one of these nine is RRYY. So within this class the fraction is 1/9; 1/16 is the fraction among all F2 plants.

q: Mendel's dihybrid F2 contained 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow and 32 wrinkled green seeds. These numbers are close to the ratio:
x: Dividing by about 35 gives roughly 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (315 : 108 : 101 : 32 of 556 seeds). This matched the ratio expected if the two genes assort independently.

q: In the F2 of Mendel's dihybrid cross, if only seed shape is considered, the ratio of round to wrinkled seeds is:
x: Round = 9 + 3 = 12 and wrinkled = 3 + 1 = 4 out of 16, giving 12 : 4 = 3 : 1. Each gene still segregates in a 3 : 1 ratio, as in a monohybrid cross.

q: The 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio of a dihybrid F2 can be explained as:
o: Two monohybrid ratios that blend together
The product of two independent 3 : 1 ratios
The result of crossing over between the two genes
x: (3 round : 1 wrinkled) × (3 yellow : 1 green) = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. Multiplying works only because the two genes are inherited independently.

q: Three independently assorting genes are crossed as AaBbCc × AaBbCc. What fraction of the offspring is expected to be recessive for all three traits (aabbcc)?
x: For each gene the chance of the homozygous recessive is 1/4, so 1/4 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/64. The 27/64 is the fraction showing all three dominant traits.

q: How many boxes are needed in a Punnett square for the cross RrYy × RrYy?
x: Each parent forms four types of gametes, so the square has 4 × 4 = 16 boxes. These 16 combinations give the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

q: In peas, tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t) and purple flower (P) is dominant to white (p). The genes assort independently. What fraction of offspring from TtPp × ttpp will be tall with white flowers?
x: Tt × tt gives tall with probability 1/2, and Pp × pp gives white (pp) with probability 1/2. Tall white = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, one of the four equal test-cross classes.

q: A pure round green pea (RRyy) is crossed with a pure wrinkled yellow pea (rrYY). In the F2, what fraction of plants shows a phenotype unlike either original parent?
x: The F2 is still 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. Here round yellow (9) and wrinkled green (1) are the new combinations: 10/16 = 5/8.

q: Which statement about independent assortment is NOT true?
o: It gives four types of gametes in equal numbers from a dihybrid
It results from the random orientation of bivalents in metaphase I
It applies to genes lying close together on the same chromosome
It produces new combinations of traits in the F2
x: Genes close together on one chromosome are linked and do not assort independently. The other statements are true of genes on different chromosomes.

q: Gene linkage is the tendency of genes that are:
o: Located on different chromosomes to be inherited together
Alleles of one gene to separate in meiosis
Located on the same chromosome to be inherited together
x: Genes on the same chromosome travel together into gametes, so they tend to be inherited as a unit. Genes on different chromosomes assort independently.

q: T. H. Morgan carried out his studies on linkage and crossing over using:
x: Morgan used the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster. His work showed that genes are carried on chromosomes and that linked genes can be separated by crossing over.

q: How many pairs of chromosomes does Drosophila melanogaster have?
x: Drosophila has 2n = 8, that is 4 pairs of chromosomes. The small number made it easy to relate genes to chromosomes. 23 pairs is the human number and 7 pairs is the pea number.

q: The number of linkage groups in an organism is equal to its:
x: All genes on one chromosome form one linkage group, and each homologous pair counts once. So the number of linkage groups equals the haploid chromosome number, for example 4 in Drosophila.

q: Crossing over is best defined as:
o: Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
Exchange of segments between sister chromatids of one chromosome
Exchange of segments between non-homologous chromosomes
Separation of homologous chromosomes during anaphase I
x: In crossing over, non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair break and exchange equal segments. Exchange between non-homologous chromosomes would be a translocation, not crossing over.

q: Crossing over takes place during:
x: Crossing over happens in prophase I, when homologous chromosomes are paired as bivalents. It does not normally happen in mitosis.

q: A chiasma (plural: chiasmata) is:
o: The centromere that holds two sister chromatids together
The point where non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes remain joined after crossing over
The point where spindle fibres attach to a chromosome
The region of a chromosome where a single gene is located
x: A chiasma is the visible X-shaped point of contact where crossing over has occurred between non-sister chromatids. The spindle attaches at the kinetochore, and the position of a gene is its locus.

q: Crossing over can occur only after:
o: Separation of sister chromatids at the centromere
Formation of the nuclear envelope around daughter nuclei
Synapsis, the pairing of homologous chromosomes into bivalents
x: Homologous chromosomes must first pair closely (synapsis) to form bivalents in prophase I. Only then can non-sister chromatids exchange segments.

q: A bivalent (tetrad) formed during prophase I of meiosis contains how many chromatids?
x: A bivalent is a pair of homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, so it has four chromatids. That is why it is also called a tetrad.

q: In a cross involving linked genes, recombinants are offspring that:
o: Show exactly the same combination of traits as one parent
Are homozygous recessive for both genes
Show new combinations of traits not present in either parent
Carry a mutation not present in either parent
x: Recombinants carry combinations of alleles produced by crossing over, unlike the parental combinations. Offspring with the parents' combinations are called parental types.

q: Recombination frequency between two linked genes is calculated as:
x: Recombination frequency is the percentage of all offspring that are recombinants. It is used as a measure of the distance between two genes on a chromosome.

q: One map unit of distance between two genes corresponds to:
x: A map unit (centimorgan) is defined as the distance that gives 1% recombinant offspring. So 12% recombination means the genes are 12 map units apart.

q: A test cross involving two linked genes gives 1000 offspring, of which 170 are recombinants. The distance between the two genes is:
x: Recombination frequency = 170 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 17%, so the genes are 17 map units apart. The 83% are parental types and do not give the map distance.

q: Which pair of linked genes would show the highest recombination frequency?
o: Two genes far apart on the same chromosome
Two genes very close together on the same chromosome
Two alleles at the same locus
x: The farther apart two genes are, the more likely a crossover will happen between them, so recombination is higher. Alleles at the same locus cannot be separated by crossing over between loci.

q: Recombination frequencies are: A–B 12%, B–C 5% and A–C 17%. The order of the genes on the chromosome is:
o: The order cannot be found from these data
x: Since the A–B distance (12) plus the B–C distance (5) equals the A–C distance (17), gene B must lie in the middle. The two outer genes are those with the largest distance between them.

q: The maximum recombination frequency observed between any two genes is:
x: Even genes very far apart on one chromosome give at most 50% recombinants, the same as unlinked genes assorting independently. So values above 50% are not seen.

q: In his linkage experiments on Drosophila, Morgan studied two traits:
x: Morgan crossed grey-bodied, long-winged flies with black-bodied, vestigial-winged flies. Seed and flower traits belong to Mendel's pea work.

q: Which of the following is NOT a reason why Drosophila was suitable for Morgan's genetic studies?
o: It has a long life cycle of several months
It produces a large number of offspring
It is easy to culture in the laboratory
It shows many easily seen mutant traits
x: Drosophila has a short life cycle of about two weeks, which allows many generations to be studied quickly. Large numbers of offspring, easy culture and visible mutants are true advantages.

q: A single crossover occurs between two gene loci in a bivalent. Of the four chromatids, how many carry a recombinant combination of these genes?
x: Crossing over involves only two non-sister chromatids, one from each homologue, so those two become recombinant. The other two chromatids keep the parental combination.

q: In a dihybrid AaBb, the alleles A and B are on one chromosome and a and b on its homologue. This arrangement is called:
x: When the two dominant alleles are on one chromosome and the two recessive alleles on the other (AB/ab), the genes are in coupling. Ab/aB would be the repulsion arrangement.

q: Morgan's studies of linkage in Drosophila supported the idea that genes:
o: Are carried on chromosomes in a linear order at fixed loci
Float freely in the cytoplasm of the cell
Are always inherited independently of each other
x: Linkage and crossing over can only be explained if genes lie in a line on chromosomes. This strongly supported the chromosome theory of inheritance.

q: The main biological importance of crossing over is that it:
o: Doubles the number of chromosomes in the gametes
Makes the sister chromatids of a chromosome identical
Produces new combinations of alleles, increasing genetic variation
x: Crossing over reshuffles alleles between homologous chromosomes, producing new combinations in gametes. This variation is raw material for natural selection.

q: Crossing over, the exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids, takes place during which substage of prophase I?
x: Homologous chromosomes pair in zygotene, and crossing over occurs in pachytene when the bivalent is fully formed. In diplotene the homologues begin to separate and the chiasmata, the visible result of crossing over, become clear.

q: Two linked genes are 20 map units apart. In a test cross producing 500 offspring, about how many recombinants are expected?
x: 20 map units means 20% recombination: 20% of 500 = 100 recombinants. The remaining 400 would be parental types.

q: The unit of distance on a genetic (linkage) map, named in honour of Morgan, is the:
x: One centimorgan equals one map unit, or 1% recombination. Angstrom is a unit of length, dalton of mass and svedberg of sedimentation rate.

q: In Drosophila, grey body is dominant to black and long wings are dominant to vestigial. Pure grey long flies are crossed with black vestigial flies. The F1 flies are:
o: Half grey long and half black vestigial
Grey vestigial and black long in equal numbers
x: The F1 receive one dominant allele of each gene from the grey long parent, so all show the dominant traits, grey body and long wings.

q: During prophase I, chiasmata first become clearly visible as homologous chromosomes begin to separate in which stage?
x: In diplotene the paired homologues start to move apart but stay joined at the chiasmata, which then become visible. Leptotene is condensation and zygotene is pairing (synapsis).

q: Which statement about crossing over is correct?
o: It normally takes place during anaphase II
It involves breakage and rejoining of non-sister chromatids
It adds new genes to a chromosome
x: In crossing over, non-sister chromatids break at the same points and rejoin with each other's segments. No new genes are added; existing alleles are reshuffled.

q: Genes A and B are 25 map units apart. A coupling dihybrid (AB/ab) is test crossed with ab/ab. What percentage of the offspring is expected to be Aabb?
x: 25% of offspring are recombinants, divided equally between Aabb and aaBb, so each is 12.5%. The parental types AaBb and aabb make up 37.5% each.

q: Linkage between two genes on the same chromosome is broken by:
x: Crossing over exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids, separating alleles that were on the same chromosome. Without it, linked genes would always stay together.

q: In a bivalent, one chromosome carries A and B and its homologue carries a and b. After a single crossover between the two loci, the four chromatids carry:
o: Two parental (AB, ab) and two recombinant (Ab, aB)
Four parental: two AB and two ab
Four recombinant: two Ab and two aB
x: The two chromatids not involved stay AB and ab. The two that crossed over exchange segments, giving Ab and aB. So one crossover gives two parental and two recombinant chromatids.

q: Two genes are completely linked in coupling (AB/ab), with no crossing over. If this dihybrid is test crossed with ab/ab, the offspring will be:
o: Only the two parental types, in a 1 : 1 ratio
x: With complete linkage AB/ab forms only AB and ab gametes, so the offspring are AaBb and aabb in equal numbers. Independent assortment would give four classes in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.

q: A dihybrid test cross gives four phenotype classes, but two classes are much more numerous than the other two. This shows that:
o: The genes are linked, and the rare classes are recombinants
The genes are unlinked and assort independently
The genes are linked, and the rare classes are parental types
The genes are completely linked with no crossing over
x: Unlinked genes would give four equal classes. An excess of two classes means the genes are linked: the common classes are parental types and the rare ones arise from crossing over.

q: A dihybrid (AB/ab) test crossed with ab/ab gives 42% AaBb, 42% aabb, 8% Aabb and 8% aaBb. The distance between genes A and B is:
x: The recombinants are Aabb and aaBb: 8% + 8% = 16%. So the genes are 16 map units apart. The 84% are parental types.

q: A test cross of AaBb × aabb gives 8% AaBb, 8% aabb, 42% Aabb and 42% aaBb. The heterozygous parent carried its alleles as:
x: The most frequent classes are the parental types, here Aabb and aaBb, so each chromosome of the parent carried the dominant allele of one gene with the recessive allele of the other (repulsion, Ab/aB). The rare classes total 16%, giving 16 map units.

q: If two genes assort independently, a dihybrid test cross (AaBb × aabb) gives what percentage of each of the four phenotypes?
x: Independent assortment gives four gamete types in equal numbers, so each of the four test-cross classes is 25%. Linkage would make the parental classes more than 25%.

q: How does crossing over modify the progeny of a dihybrid whose two genes are linked?
o: It makes all offspring identical to the parents
It produces a small proportion of offspring with new (recombinant) combinations
It produces recombinants in more than half of the offspring
It changes dominant alleles into recessive alleles
x: Without crossing over, linked genes would give only parental combinations. Crossing over in some meiotic cells creates recombinant gametes, so a minority of offspring show new combinations, always less than half.

q: A dihybrid F2 shows the four expected phenotypes, but with too many parental types and too few new combinations compared with 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. This is explained by:
o: Independent assortment of the two genes
Linkage of the two genes on the same chromosome
The two genes being on different chromosomes
x: Linked genes tend to stay in their parental combinations, so new combinations are fewer than independent assortment predicts. Genes on different chromosomes would give 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

q: Two genes are completely linked in coupling (AB/ab), with complete dominance and no crossing over. If this dihybrid is self-crossed, the F2 phenotypic ratio is:
x: Each parent forms only AB and ab gametes, giving 1 AB/AB : 2 AB/ab : 1 ab/ab. Phenotypically this is 3 dominant for both traits : 1 recessive for both, like a monohybrid ratio.

q: As the distance between two linked genes on a chromosome increases:
o: Recombination decreases and linkage becomes stronger
Recombination stays the same at every distance
The genes become alleles of each other
Recombination increases and inheritance comes closer to independent assortment
x: A larger distance allows more crossovers between the genes, so more recombinants form. Very distant genes (near 50% recombination) behave almost as if unlinked.

q: Genes A and B are linked in coupling (AB/ab) with a recombination frequency of 10%. The expected proportions of gametes are:
o: 25% each of AB, ab, Ab and aB
x: 10% of gametes are recombinant, shared equally between Ab and aB (5% each). The remaining 90% are parental, 45% AB and 45% ab.

q: For two linked genes in a dihybrid, which statement is correct?
o: All four gamete types are formed in equal numbers
Recombinant gametes are more frequent than parental gametes
Parental-type gametes are more frequent than recombinant gametes
x: Crossing over between the genes happens in only some meiotic cells, and even then only two of four chromatids are recombinant. So parental gametes always outnumber recombinants.

q: A dihybrid test cross is expected to give a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio when the two genes are:
o: Located at neighbouring loci on one chromosome
x: Genes on different chromosomes assort independently, giving four equal gamete types and a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 test-cross ratio. Linked genes give an excess of parental types.

q: In a test cross AB/ab × ab/ab, the recombinant offspring arise from crossing over in:
x: The ab/ab parent forms only ab gametes whether or not crossing over occurs, so it cannot create new combinations. Recombinants come from Ab and aB gametes of the heterozygous parent.

q: If no crossing over occurs between two linked genes, how many types of gametes does a coupling dihybrid (AB/ab) produce?
x: Without crossing over, the chromosomes pass on intact, so only AB and ab gametes are formed. Unlinked genes would give four gamete types.

q: Which of the following does NOT produce new combinations of alleles in gametes?
o: Crossing over between two linked genes
Random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I
x: With complete linkage the alleles on a chromosome always stay together, so only parental combinations pass on. Crossing over and independent assortment both create new combinations.

q: A test cross of AB/ab × ab/ab gives 460 AaBb, 440 aabb, 52 Aabb and 48 aaBb offspring. The recombination frequency between A and B is:
x: Recombinants are Aabb and aaBb: 52 + 48 = 100 out of 1000 total, so 10%. The 900 parental-type offspring show that the genes are linked.

q: A dihybrid with linked genes in coupling (AB/ab) undergoes crossing over between the genes. The recombinant gametes are:
o: AB and ab, the parental combinations
Ab and aB, the new combinations
Aa and Bb, each with both alleles of a gene
x: In coupling, the parental chromosomes are AB and ab, so crossing over makes the new combinations Ab and aB. A gamete carries one allele of each gene, never Aa or Bb.

q: A dihybrid with linked genes in repulsion (Ab/aB) undergoes crossing over between the genes. The recombinant gametes are:
o: Ab and aB, the parental combinations
AB and ab, the new combinations
Aa and Bb, each with both alleles of a gene
x: In repulsion the parental chromosomes are Ab and aB, so crossing over between them produces AB and ab. Which gametes count as recombinant depends on the parental arrangement.

q: In Morgan's test cross of grey long (heterozygous) Drosophila, a small number of grey vestigial and black long flies appeared. Morgan explained these as the result of:
o: Crossing over between the linked genes
x: Most offspring were parental types (grey long and black vestigial), showing linkage. The few new combinations arose because crossing over had separated the linked alleles in some gametes.

q: Genes A and B are 20 map units apart. A coupling dihybrid (AB/ab) is test crossed with ab/ab. What percentage of the offspring is expected to be aabb?
x: Recombinants are 20%, so parental types are 80%, divided equally between AaBb and aabb: 40% each. The value 10% is one recombinant class.

q: Gene linkage counters independent assortment because linked alleles:
o: Tend to move together into the same gamete
Fuse together into a single allele
x: Linked alleles sit on the same chromosome, so they usually enter the same gamete together. This prevents the free reshuffling that genes on different chromosomes show.

q: Three linked genes lie in the order P–Q–R. The recombination frequency is 10% for P–Q and 15% for Q–R. Ignoring double crossovers, the expected recombination frequency between P and R is about:
x: Map distances along a chromosome add up: 10 + 15 = 25 map units between the outer genes P and R. A difference (5%) would apply only if R lay between P and Q.

q: In Drosophila, a grey long female (BV/bv) is test crossed with a black vestigial male. If 17% of the offspring are recombinants, what percentage is expected to be grey vestigial?
x: The two recombinant classes, grey vestigial and black long, share the 17% equally, so each is 8.5%. Each parental class (grey long or black vestigial) is 41.5%.

q: A dihybrid test cross gives 48% AaBb, 48% aabb, 2% Aabb and 2% aaBb. These results show that genes A and B are:
o: Completely linked with no crossing over
x: Recombinants are 2% + 2% = 4%, so the genes are closely linked, about 4 map units apart. Some recombinants did appear, so linkage is not complete.

q: In 30% of meiotic cells of a dihybrid, one crossover occurs between two linked genes; in the rest, none occurs. What is the expected recombination frequency between these genes?
x: Each crossover involves only two of the four chromatids, so a cell with one crossover gives half recombinant gametes. Recombinant gametes are therefore 30% × 1/2 = 15%.

q: Crossing over between sister chromatids does not produce new combinations of alleles because sister chromatids:
o: Are never joined at a centromere
Carry different genes at each locus
x: Sister chromatids are copies made by DNA replication, so exchange between them swaps identical segments. Only exchange between non-sister chromatids of homologues can bring together different alleles.

q: Two genes are completely linked in repulsion (Ab/aB). If this dihybrid is test crossed with ab/ab, the offspring will be:
o: Only double-dominant and double-recessive types (AaBb, aabb), 1 : 1
All four types in equal numbers
Only the two single-dominant types (Aabb, aaBb), 1 : 1
x: With no crossing over, Ab/aB forms only Ab and aB gametes. Combined with ab, these give Aabb and aaBb in equal numbers. AaBb and aabb would be recombinants here.

q: Gene linkage is an exception to Mendel's law of:
x: Linked genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, so they do not assort independently. The alleles of each linked gene still segregate normally.

q: In a dihybrid test cross, two genes give a recombination frequency of 50%. This means the genes:
o: Assort as if they were unlinked
Are tightly linked, very close together
Are alleles of the same gene
x: 50% recombination gives four equal classes, exactly as for genes that assort independently. Tightly linked genes would give very few recombinants.

q: An important effect of gene linkage is that it:
o: Increases the number of different gamete types
Keeps parental combinations of alleles together through generations
Ensures a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio in every dihybrid F2
Separates the two alleles of the same gene
x: Linkage holds alleles on one chromosome together, so useful parental combinations tend to be passed on intact. It reduces, rather than increases, the variety of gametes.

q: In a test cross involving linked genes, offspring that show the same combination of traits as the parents are called:
x: Offspring with the original combinations of linked alleles are parental types. Those with new combinations produced by crossing over are recombinants.

q: How many autosomes are present in a normal human somatic cell?
x: A human somatic cell has 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs (44) of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. 46 is the total, and 23 is the number in a gamete.

q: The sex chromosomes of a normal human male are:
x: Human males have one X and one Y chromosome (44 + XY). Females are XX; XO is the male condition of grasshoppers, and ZW is the female condition of birds.

q: In humans, the sex of a child is decided by:
o: The kind of sperm, X- or Y-bearing, that fertilises the egg
The kind of egg, X- or Y-bearing, that is fertilised
The number of autosomes received from the mother
The number of autosomes received from the father
x: Every egg carries an X, so the sperm decides: an X-bearing sperm gives a girl (XX) and a Y-bearing sperm gives a boy (XY). Eggs never carry a Y chromosome.

q: The human male is called the heterogametic sex because he:
o: Produces two kinds of sperm, X-bearing and Y-bearing
Has more autosomes than the female
x: A male (XY) forms two kinds of gametes for sex chromosomes in equal numbers. The female (XX) forms only X-bearing eggs, so she is homogametic. Both sexes have 44 autosomes.

q: What is the probability that a couple's next child will be a boy?
x: Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y, so each child has a 1/2 chance of being a boy (XY), whatever the sexes of the earlier children.

q: A couple plans three children. What is the probability that all three will be girls?
x: Each birth is independent with a 1/2 chance of a girl, so the chance of three girls is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

q: A couple has four children. What is the probability that exactly two are boys and two are girls?
x: Any one order (for example boy, boy, girl, girl) has probability (1/2)^4 = 1/16. There are 6 different orders with two boys and two girls, so the probability is 6/16 = 3/8, not 1/2.

q: In birds, which sex is heterogametic?
x: Birds use the ZZ–ZW system: males are ZZ (homogametic) and females are ZW (heterogametic). So in birds it is the egg, not the sperm, that decides sex.

q: In grasshoppers, which use the XX–XO system, the male:
o: Has one X and one Y chromosome
Has only one X chromosome and no Y
Has two X chromosomes and no Y
x: In the XX–XO system the female is XX and the male has a single X with no partner (XO). The male therefore has one chromosome fewer than the female.

q: Chromosomes that are alike in males and females and are not involved in sex determination are called:
x: Autosomes are the 22 pairs that are the same in both sexes. Sex chromosomes (allosomes) are the X and Y, which differ between males and females.

q: A normal human egg cell contains:
x: An egg is haploid: 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome. Since the mother is XX, that sex chromosome is always an X, never a Y.

q: Which pair of chromosome sets can be found in normal human sperm?
x: Meiosis in a 44 + XY male separates X from Y, so half the sperm are 22 + X and half are 22 + Y. Sperm are haploid, so 44 autosomes is wrong.

q: Which statement about the human X and Y chromosomes is correct?
o: The Y is larger and carries more genes than the X
The X and Y carry exactly the same set of genes
The X is larger and carries many genes, while the Y is small and carries few
Only the Y carries genes; the X is genetically inactive
x: The X chromosome is large and carries many genes for ordinary body functions, such as colour vision and clotting. The Y is small and carries only a few genes, mainly for maleness.

q: A human male is said to be hemizygous for X-linked genes because he:
o: Has two identical copies of each X-linked gene
Has two different alleles of each X-linked gene
Has only one copy of each X-linked gene
Has no X-linked genes at all
x: Hemizygous means having only one allele of a gene. A male has one X, and the Y does not carry matching alleles, so each X-linked gene is present once.

q: Why does a single recessive X-linked allele show its effect in a male?
o: The Y chromosome carries a dominant allele that is switched off
Recessive alleles are dominant in males
Male hormones change the recessive allele into a dominant one
The Y chromosome carries no corresponding allele to mask it
x: A male is hemizygous: the Y has no partner allele for most X-linked genes, so nothing can mask a recessive allele on his only X. In a female the second X can carry a dominant allele.

q: A gene found only on the Y chromosome is passed from:
o: A father to all his daughters
A father to all his sons
A mother to all her sons
A mother to all her daughters
x: Only males carry a Y, and every son receives his father's Y. So Y-linked genes pass from father to all sons and never to daughters.

q: A man has an X-linked allele. To which of his children will he pass it?
o: All of his sons and none of his daughters
Half of his sons and half of his daughters
All of his daughters and none of his sons
x: A father gives his only X to every daughter and his Y to every son. So an X-linked allele goes to all his daughters and never directly to a son.

q: A man's single X chromosome was inherited from his:
o: Father or mother with equal chance
x: A son gets the Y from his father, so his X must come from his mother. This is why X-linked traits in males are inherited through the mother.

q: A woman's two X chromosomes were inherited:
o: One from her father and one from her paternal grandfather
One from her mother and one from her father
x: Every child gets one sex chromosome from each parent. A daughter gets an X from her mother and her father's single X, so one X comes from each parent.

q: From which grandparent did a girl inherit the X chromosome that her father gave her?
o: Either paternal grandparent with equal chance
x: The father's only X came from his own mother, because his father gave him a Y. So the X a girl receives from her father always comes from her paternal grandmother.

q: Sex-linked genes are genes that are:
x: Sex-linked genes are carried on the sex chromosomes (X or Y). Many of them, like those for colour vision and clotting, have nothing to do with sex organs.

q: In a human male cell, which chromosome pair is NOT fully homologous?
o: The sex chromosome pair, X and Y
x: In males the X and Y differ greatly in size and gene content, so they are not a fully homologous pair. Each autosome pair consists of two similar homologues.

q: A person with 44 autosomes plus XXY develops as a male. This shows that in humans:
o: The number of X chromosomes determines maleness
The presence of a Y chromosome determines maleness
Having more than one X always gives a female
x: Even with two X chromosomes, the presence of a Y makes the person male. So in humans the Y chromosome, not the number of X chromosomes, decides maleness.

q: Which of the following genes is located on the human X chromosome?
o: The gene for hairy ear rims (hypertrichosis)
The gene for red–green colour vision
The gene for ABO blood groups
x: Red–green colour vision is controlled by an X-linked gene. Hairy ear rims is a Y-linked (holandric) trait, while ABO blood groups and albinism are controlled by autosomal genes.

q: Why are boys and girls born in roughly equal numbers?
o: Males produce X-bearing and Y-bearing sperm in equal numbers
Females produce X-bearing and Y-bearing eggs in equal numbers
Every second egg carries a Y chromosome
Autosomes decide sex in half of all births
x: Meiosis in an XY male gives equal numbers of X- and Y-bearing sperm, so fertilisation gives about 1 girl : 1 boy. Eggs always carry an X.

q: Which pattern points to a recessive gene being X-linked rather than autosomal?
o: The trait appears equally in both sexes
The trait is much more common in males than in females
The trait passes directly from father to son
The trait never skips a generation
x: Males need only one recessive X-linked allele to show the trait, while females need two, so X-linked recessive traits are much commoner in males. Autosomal traits affect both sexes equally, and father-to-son passing rules out X-linkage.

q: For an X-linked gene with two alleles, how many genotypes are possible in males and in females?
x: Males have one X, so they can only be XᴬY or XᵃY (2 genotypes). Females have two X chromosomes, so they can be XᴬXᴬ, XᴬXᵃ or XᵃXᵃ (3 genotypes).

q: Inheritance of an X-linked gene is called sex-linked because:
o: It only controls the development of sex organs
It is expressed only in females
It is always passed from father to son
Its pattern differs between sexes, as males have one X and females two
x: Males carry one X and females two, so an X-linked gene is inherited and expressed differently in the two sexes. Most X-linked genes do not control sex organs.

q: A man carries a recessive allele on his X chromosome. What fraction of his sperm carry this allele?
x: Half his sperm receive the X (carrying the allele) and half receive the Y. So 1/2 of his sperm carry the allele, and all of those will produce daughters.

q: Compared with the human X chromosome, the Y chromosome:
o: Is smaller and carries mainly genes for male development
Is larger and carries genes for colour vision
Is the same size and carries the same genes
Is found in both males and females
x: The Y chromosome is small and carries few genes, chiefly those that direct testis formation and male development. Colour-vision genes are on the X, and only males have a Y.

q: Human females are described as homogametic because they:
o: Produce eggs with either X or Y chromosomes
Produce only one kind of egg, each with an X chromosome
x: A female is XX, so every egg she produces carries one X. Producing a single kind of gamete for sex chromosomes is what homogametic means.

q: Two reciprocal crosses for a trait give different results in the F1 sons. The gene is most probably located on:
o: A pair of linked genes on one autosome
x: Autosomal genes, linked or not and whatever their dominance, give the same result in both sexes of reciprocal crosses. Different results that depend on which parent carried the trait, especially in the sons, are typical of X-linked genes.

q: Red–green colour blindness in humans is inherited as a:
x: The allele for red–green colour blindness is recessive and lies on the X chromosome. This is why it is much more common in men than in women.

q: A woman who carries the colour-blindness allele marries a man with normal vision. What proportion of their sons are expected to be colour-blind?
x: The mother has one normal X and one colour-blind X. Each son gets his X from her, so half the sons get the colour-blind X and are affected. The father gives his sons only a Y.

q: A carrier woman for colour blindness marries a man with normal vision. What proportion of their daughters are expected to be carriers?
x: Every daughter gets the father's normal X. From the mother she gets either the normal or the colour-blind X with equal chance, so 1/2 the daughters are carriers and none is colour-blind.

q: A colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous for normal vision. Their children are expected to be:
o: Colour-blind sons and normal non-carrier daughters
Sons with normal vision and daughters who are carriers
Half the sons colour-blind and half the daughters carriers
x: The father gives his colour-blind X to every daughter, making them carriers, and his Y to every son. Sons get a normal X from their mother, so they see normally.

q: A colour-blind man marries a carrier woman. What is the probability that their first child will be a colour-blind daughter?
x: The chance of a daughter is 1/2. A daughter always gets the father's colour-blind X and has a 1/2 chance of getting the mother's colour-blind X, so 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

q: A colour-blind woman marries a man with normal vision. What will their children be like?
o: All sons colour-blind and all daughters carriers
All sons normal and all daughters colour-blind
Half the sons colour-blind and half the daughters carriers
x: The mother has two colour-blind X chromosomes, so every son receives one and is colour-blind. Every daughter also gets the father's normal X, so she is a carrier with normal vision.

q: Criss-cross inheritance of an X-linked recessive trait means that it passes from:
o: A father directly to all his sons
A mother directly to all her daughters
A grandfather to his son's sons only
A father, through his daughter, to his grandson
x: An affected man passes his X to his daughter, who is an unaffected carrier, and she can pass it to her son, who shows the trait. The trait thus crosses from one sex to the other in each generation.

q: A colour-blind boy has two parents with normal vision. From whom did he inherit the colour-blindness allele?
o: His mother, who is a carrier
His father, who is a carrier
Neither parent; boys always develop it
x: A son gets his X only from his mother, so the allele came from her. With normal vision herself, she must be a heterozygous carrier. The father gave the boy a Y.

q: A woman with normal vision has a colour-blind father. She marries a man with normal vision. What is the probability that a daughter of theirs will be colour-blind?
x: The woman must be a carrier, since her father gave her his colour-blind X. But every daughter gets the husband's normal X, so no daughter can be colour-blind; half will be carriers.

q: A woman is red–green colour-blind. Which of the following must be true?
o: All her daughters will be colour-blind
x: She has two colour-blind X chromosomes, and one came from her father, whose only X must therefore carry the allele, so he is colour-blind. Her mother could be just a carrier, and her daughters depend on their father.

q: Red–green colour blindness is more common in men than in women because:
o: The allele is dominant in men and recessive in women
The allele is carried on the Y chromosome
Men need only one recessive allele to be affected, women need two
x: Men have one X, so one recessive allele is enough. Women are affected only if both X chromosomes carry it, which is far less likely. The gene is on the X, not the Y.

q: Sex-linked inheritance of white eye colour in Drosophila was first studied by:
x: Thomas Hunt Morgan found a white-eyed male fruit fly and showed by crosses that the eye-colour gene lies on the X chromosome. Mendel worked with garden peas and knew nothing of sex linkage.

q: A homozygous red-eyed female Drosophila is crossed with a white-eyed male. The F1 will be:
o: All red-eyed, both males and females
Half red-eyed and half white-eyed in each sex
x: The female is XᴿXᴿ and gives Xᴿ to every offspring. Daughters are XᴿXʷ and sons are XᴿY, so all F1 flies have red eyes, since red is dominant.

q: In Morgan's cross, red-eyed F1 Drosophila (from a red-eyed female and a white-eyed male) were interbred. In the F2, the white-eyed flies were:
x: F1 is XᴿXʷ × XᴿY. All F2 females get Xᴿ from the father and are red-eyed. Half the F2 males get Xʷ from the mother and are white-eyed, so all white-eyed flies are males.

q: A white-eyed female Drosophila is crossed with a red-eyed male. What will the F1 be?
x: The female is XʷXʷ and the male XᴿY. Daughters get Xᴿ from the father and are red-eyed (XᴿXʷ). Sons get Xʷ from the mother and are white-eyed (XʷY). This is criss-cross inheritance.

q: The F1 from a white-eyed female × red-eyed male Drosophila cross are interbred. What proportion of the F2 females are white-eyed?
x: The F1 cross is XᴿXʷ × XʷY. Every F2 female gets Xʷ from the father and Xᴿ or Xʷ from the mother, so half are XᴿXʷ (red) and half XʷXʷ (white).

q: Which statement about the white-eye gene of Drosophila is correct?
o: It is on the Y chromosome and is passed only to sons
It is on an autosome and appears equally in both sexes
It is dominant to the red-eye allele
It is on the X chromosome and has no allele on the Y
x: Morgan showed that the white-eye allele is recessive and lies on the X, with no matching allele on the Y. So males show it with a single copy, while females need two.

q: Holandric traits are those controlled by genes on the:
x: Holandric (Y-linked) genes are carried only on the Y chromosome. They appear only in males and pass from father to every son.

q: Which of the following is an example of a holandric (Y-linked) trait in humans?
o: Hairy ear rims (hypertrichosis of the pinna)
x: Hairy ear rims is the textbook example of a Y-linked trait, passed only from father to son. Hemophilia and colour blindness are X-linked, and albinism is autosomal.

q: A man shows a holandric trait. What is the probability that his daughter will show it?
x: Holandric genes are on the Y chromosome, and a daughter never receives her father's Y. So none of his daughters can show the trait, though all his sons will.

q: A man has a Y-linked trait. What is the probability that his daughter's son will show the trait?
x: His daughter gets his X, not his Y, so she does not carry the Y-linked gene. Her son gets his Y from his own father, so he cannot inherit it from this grandfather.

q: A carrier of an X-linked recessive trait is:
o: A heterozygous female with normal phenotype
A male with the recessive allele
x: A carrier has one normal and one recessive allele (heterozygous) and shows no symptoms, but can pass the allele on. A male with the allele is affected, not a carrier.

q: Which statement about carriers of an X-linked recessive trait is correct?
o: Carriers are females, because a male with the allele always shows the trait
Carriers are usually males, because they have only one X
Carriers always show a mild form of the trait
Carriers can pass the allele only to their daughters
x: A male is hemizygous, so his single allele always shows: he is affected or normal, never a carrier. A carrier female can pass the allele to sons and daughters alike.

q: Two parents with normal vision have a colour-blind son. What is the probability that their next son will also be colour-blind?
x: The first son shows that the mother is a carrier. Each son has a 1/2 chance of getting her colour-blind X, and earlier births do not change this chance.

q: If both parents are red–green colour-blind, what proportion of their children are expected to be colour-blind?
x: The mother has two colour-blind X chromosomes and the father one. Sons get a colour-blind X from the mother, and daughters get one from each parent, so every child is colour-blind.

q: A woman with normal vision has a colour-blind brother, and both their parents have normal vision. What is the probability that she is a carrier?
x: Her brother shows that their mother is a carrier (XᴺXⁿ) and the father is XᴺY. The woman got Xᴺ from her father and Xᴺ or Xⁿ from her mother, so her chance of being a carrier is 1/2.

q: A red-eyed female Drosophila crossed with a white-eyed male gives some white-eyed daughters. The female's genotype must be:
o: Heterozygous, with one red and one white allele
x: A white-eyed daughter needs Xʷ from both parents, so the red-eyed mother must carry Xʷ along with Xᴿ. A homozygous red mother would give only red-eyed daughters, and a female cannot be hemizygous for an X gene.

q: Which of the following traits shows criss-cross inheritance?
x: Criss-cross inheritance is shown by X-linked recessive traits such as colour blindness. Hairy ear rims is Y-linked (father to son only), while ABO groups and albinism are autosomal.

q: A person with red–green colour blindness has difficulty in:
o: Telling red and green colours apart
x: Red–green colour blindness reduces the ability to distinguish red from green. Night blindness is poor vision in dim light, and myopia is poor distance vision.

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of X-linked recessive inheritance?
o: Affected males are much more common than affected females
An affected male's daughters are at least carriers
The trait can skip a generation through carrier females
An affected father passes the trait to all his sons
x: A father gives his Y, not his X, to his sons, so he cannot pass an X-linked trait to them. The other three features are typical of X-linked recessive traits.

q: A Y-linked trait in humans will appear in:
o: Only females, and in every daughter of an affected mother
Only males, and in every son of an affected father
Only the daughters of an affected father
x: Only males have a Y chromosome, and every son of an affected father gets that Y. So a Y-linked trait shows only in males and runs straight down the male line.

q: Morgan's crosses with white-eyed Drosophila provided evidence that:
o: Genes are located in the cytoplasm
Eye colour in flies is inherited only through females
A specific gene is carried on a specific chromosome, the X
x: The white-eye results followed the X chromosome exactly from generation to generation. This linked a particular gene to a particular chromosome and supported the chromosome theory of inheritance.

q: Hemophilia is a hereditary disorder in which:
o: Red and green colours cannot be told apart
x: In hemophilia a clotting factor is missing or faulty, so blood takes a long time to clot and wounds bleed for long. Sickle shape, colour blindness and albinism are other genetic disorders.

q: Hemophilia A is caused by a deficiency of clotting factor:
x: Hemophilia A, the commonest form, results from lack of factor VIII (antihemophilic factor). Lack of factor IX causes hemophilia B.

q: Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) results from a deficiency of clotting factor:
x: Hemophilia B is due to lack of factor IX, also called Christmas factor. Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A. Both genes lie on the X chromosome.

q: The inheritance of hemophilia in humans is:
x: The hemophilia gene is recessive and located on the X chromosome, with no allele on the Y. It therefore follows the same pattern as red–green colour blindness.

q: Why is hemophilia far more common in males than in females?
o: A male needs only one recessive allele, a female needs two
The allele is on the Y chromosome
Females have no clotting factors on their X chromosome
x: Males have a single X, so one recessive allele causes the disease. A female is affected only with two recessive alleles, one from each parent, which is rare.

q: A carrier woman marries a normal man. What proportion of their sons are expected to have hemophilia?
x: The mother is XᴴXʰ and every son gets one of her X chromosomes, so half the sons get Xʰ and are hemophilic. The father gives his sons only a Y.

q: A carrier woman marries a normal man. What is the probability that a child of theirs will be a hemophilic daughter?
x: Every daughter gets the father's normal Xᴴ, so she can be normal or a carrier but never hemophilic. The probability of a hemophilic daughter is therefore 0.

q: A carrier woman marries a normal man. What is the probability that their first child will be a hemophilic son?
x: The chance of a son is 1/2, and the chance a son gets the mother's Xʰ is 1/2. So the probability of a hemophilic son is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

q: A hemophilic man marries a woman who is not a carrier. Their children are expected to be:
x: The father gives Xʰ to every daughter, who also gets Xᴴ from her mother, so all daughters are carriers. The sons get his Y and their mother's Xᴴ, so they are normal.

q: Why can a hemophilic father NOT pass hemophilia to his son?
o: His son receives two of his X chromosomes
He gives his son a Y chromosome, which lacks the gene
The hemophilia allele is lost during meiosis in males
The allele is dominant only in females
x: A son receives the Y chromosome from his father and his X from his mother. The hemophilia allele is on the father's X, so it goes to daughters, not sons.

q: A hemophilic man marries a carrier woman. What proportion of their daughters are expected to be hemophilic?
x: Every daughter gets Xʰ from the father. From the carrier mother she gets Xᴴ or Xʰ with equal chance, so 1/2 of daughters are XʰXʰ (hemophilic) and 1/2 are carriers.

q: A hemophilic man marries a carrier woman. What proportion of all their children are expected to have normal clotting?
x: Half the sons get Xᴴ from the mother and are normal, and half the daughters are carriers (XᴴXʰ) with normal clotting. So 1/2 of all children clot normally.

q: For a girl to be born with hemophilia, which must be true of her parents?
o: Her mother is hemophilic and her father is normal
Her father is hemophilic and her mother is at least a carrier
Only her mother needs to be a carrier
x: A hemophilic girl needs Xʰ from both parents. Her father's single X must be Xʰ, so he is hemophilic, and her mother must carry at least one Xʰ. Males cannot be carriers.

q: Hemophilia spread through several European royal families from:
o: A king of Spain who had hemophilia
A Russian tsar who was a carrier
Queen Victoria of England, who was a carrier
A princess who had two hemophilia alleles
x: Queen Victoria was a carrier. Through her carrier daughters the allele reached the royal families of Spain, Russia and Germany, which is why hemophilia was called the royal disease.

q: Which feature is typical of a person with hemophilia?
o: Inability to distinguish red from green
Lack of pigment in skin and hair
Prolonged bleeding even after a minor cut
x: Because a clotting factor is missing, blood clots slowly and small cuts, tooth extractions or internal injuries can bleed for a long time. The other features belong to other inherited disorders.

q: Two parents with normal clotting have a hemophilic son. The mother's genotype must be:
x: The son's Xʰ came from his mother. Since she clots normally, she must also carry Xᴴ, so she is a heterozygous carrier. XʰXʰ would make her hemophilic, and XᴴY is a male genotype.

q: A normal woman has a hemophilic brother; their parents are normal. She marries a normal man. What is the probability that their first son will be hemophilic?
x: Her mother must be a carrier, so the woman has a 1/2 chance of being a carrier. If she is, each son has a 1/2 chance of hemophilia. So 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

q: A normal woman whose father was hemophilic marries a normal man. What proportion of their sons are expected to be hemophilic?
x: Her father gave her his Xʰ, so she is certainly a carrier. Each son gets one of her two X chromosomes, so half the sons are expected to be hemophilic.

q: A female with hemophilia has the genotype:
x: A female shows this recessive disorder only when both X chromosomes carry the allele (XʰXʰ). XᴴXʰ is a carrier, and XʰY is a hemophilic male.

q: The gene for hemophilia is located:
o: On both the X and Y chromosomes
On the X chromosome, with no corresponding allele on the Y
x: The hemophilia gene lies on the X chromosome and the Y carries no matching allele. This is why males are hemizygous for it and are affected by a single recessive allele.

q: What fraction of the eggs of a woman who is a carrier for hemophilia carry the hemophilia allele?
x: A carrier is XᴴXʰ. In meiosis the two X chromosomes separate, so half her eggs carry Xᴴ and half carry Xʰ.

q: A hemophilic man's daughter, who clots normally, marries a normal man. What proportion of her sons are expected to be hemophilic?
x: The daughter received her father's Xʰ, so she is a carrier. Each of her sons has a 1/2 chance of getting that Xʰ, so half are expected to be hemophilic: the trait skips to the grandsons.

q: A boy has hemophilia, but both his parents clot normally. Which relative could also have had hemophilia and been the source of the allele?
x: The boy's Xʰ came from his carrier mother, who could have received it from her own father, a hemophilic maternal grandfather. The father's side gave the boy only a Y, and his father is normal.

q: In hemophilia, a clot forms very slowly because:
o: Platelets are completely absent from the blood
The blood contains too much vitamin K
Red blood cells are too few to form a clot
A clotting factor needed for fibrin formation is deficient
x: Clotting needs a chain of clotting factors that finally turn fibrinogen into fibrin threads. If factor VIII or IX is missing, this chain is slowed and fibrin forms slowly.

q: Hemophilia and red–green colour blindness are alike in that both are:
o: Caused by genes on the Y chromosome
Commoner in females than in males
x: Both genes are recessive and lie on the X chromosome. So both show criss-cross inheritance, appear mostly in males and are passed on by carrier females.

q: Bleeding episodes in hemophilia are treated by:
o: Giving extra red blood cells only
Giving the missing clotting factor, such as factor VIII
x: Patients are given the clotting factor they lack, for example factor VIII concentrate in hemophilia A, which allows normal clotting for a time. This treats bleeding but does not cure the gene defect.

q: A carrier woman and a normal man have three sons. What is the probability that all three sons have normal clotting?
x: Each son independently has a 1/2 chance of getting the mother's Xᴴ and being normal. For all three sons this is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

q: Which statement about the inheritance of hemophilia is correct?
o: A carrier man can pass hemophilia to his sons
A hemophilic woman can have normal sons with a normal husband
A man cannot inherit hemophilia from his father
A normal father can have a hemophilic daughter
x: A son gets his X from his mother, so hemophilia never passes from father to son. Males cannot be carriers, a hemophilic woman gives Xʰ to every son, and a daughter of a normal father always gets his Xᴴ.

q: Which of the following genotypes can NOT exist for the hemophilia gene?
x: The Y chromosome carries no allele for the hemophilia gene, so a genotype like XʰYʰ is impossible. XʰY is a hemophilic male, XᴴXʰ a carrier female and XʰXʰ a hemophilic female.

q: A hemophilic man marries a carrier woman. What is the probability that their first child will be a carrier daughter?
x: The chance of a daughter is 1/2. She always gets Xʰ from her father and has a 1/2 chance of getting Xᴴ from her mother (making her a carrier), so 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

q: A woman with normal clotting and a normal husband have two hemophilic sons. What proportion of their daughters are expected to be carriers?
x: The hemophilic sons show the mother is a carrier (XᴴXʰ). Each daughter gets the father's Xᴴ and has a 1/2 chance of getting the mother's Xʰ, so 1/2 of daughters are carriers.
